fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, “As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.” (Psalm 42:1). He isn't longing for something God hands out. He's longing for God. Think of me staring at the oven window while a batch bakes, except his longing is aimed at the best possible target.

Close, but this psalm never mentions a long life. Right after the deer, the writer says his soul thirsts “…for God, the living God.” (Psalm 42:2). He also says his tears have been his food both day and night (Psalm 42:3). The longing is for God, not for more days.

The writer asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). That's a question about when, and the verse doesn't say he's standing in God's presence yet. He's thirsting for the living God, and the question is how he puts that longing into words. So the card's statement says more than the text does.

Right, it's False. The writer asks, “When shall I come and appear in God’s presence?” (Psalm 42:2). That's a question about a time to come, and the verse doesn't say he's already standing in God's presence. I think the thirst in that verse is something he feels strongly.

Weeping shows up in a different verse. Right before this, he says his tears have been his food day and night (Psalm 42:3). What he remembers about the procession is leading it to the house of God “…with shouts of joy and praise.” (Psalm 42:4). Shouts of joy and praise are the words the verse gives us for that walk.

That's right. The writer says, “…my soul despairs within me. Therefore I remember You from the land of Jordan and the peaks of Hermon…” (Psalm 42:6). Look at that word “Therefore.” The despair is tied right to the remembering. He tells God he remembers Him instead of letting go.

True. He says, “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me.” (Psalm 42:7). Your waterfalls, Your breakers, Your waves. It's a picture of how heavy it all feels, and he's telling God whose waves they are.
That's a cozy guess, baker, but dreams don't appear in this verse. What's with him at night is “His song,” and it's “…a prayer to the God of my life.” (Psalm 42:8). A song is the word the verse uses.
He does ask hard questions in this psalm. Still, what he says is, “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy.” (Psalm 43:4). The word he lands on is joy, and he says it about God.

The text says the opposite. He says, “Then I will go to the altar of God, to God, my greatest joy. I will praise You with the harp, O God, my God.” (Psalm 43:4). Praising with a harp is a plan with sound in it. Silence isn't what he says.
Good instrument, baker, but it's not the one he names. He says he'll praise God “…with the harp…” (Psalm 43:4). No tambourine in these verses.
